group.passage:
In a remote village surrounded by jagged hills, life unfolded in simple yet arduous ways. The villagers shared <u>a strong bond</u>, yet their lives were dictated by their harsh environment. Narrow dirt paths wound precariously through rocky terrain, making obtaining even the most basic necessities a daily struggle. There, distance was not merely a measure of kilometers; rather, it was <u>an invisible wall</u>, cutting them off from the possibilities of another world.
Amid the mountains stood a man named Dashrath Manjhi, unaware that his life would later be transformed. One day, his wife perished in a dreadful accident on the perilous trail leading to the village. Overwhelmed with sorrow, he resolved to carve a passage through the stone barriers to reach the more prosperous towns beyond. He told people about his strong ambition, but he was soon dismissed by those around him as a madman for embarking on an impossible mission. Nevertheless, Manjhi took up a hammer and a chisel, vowing to confront the mountains that had long controlled the villagers’ fate.
Day after day, year after year, he fought bravely against <u>the unyielding monster</u>, enduring monsoon rains and the blistering sun. Selling his few goats to buy tools, he worked morning and evening—before and after his day job as a laborer. After twenty-two relentless years, the road he carved shrank the distance between isolation and opportunity from fifty kilometers to ten. His feat earned him the title of “Mountain Man,” and the path he created became known as a monument of love, drawing tourists and admiration from across the world.
Yet, beneath <u>the huge reverence</u> lies a quiet irony. While his story inspired films and memorials, Manjhi’s family still live in poverty, struggling as wage laborers in the very village his labor transformed. The movie about his life earned praise and profit, but his descendants reportedly received only a meager payment from the filmmakers—barely enough to build a house. Perhaps the true mountain was not the one he carved through, but the indifference of a society quick to praise a legend, yet slow to uplift the lives left behind.

options.D: They supported him and were optimistic about his project.
